text: You already know not to tune on the test set. But there is a subtler trap. If you tune long enough against your cross-validation folds, the validation score itself stops being honest. This lesson shows why, and how to get an estimate you can trust.

Every dataset has a job. The training rows fit the parameters. The validation folds compare models and tune hyperparameters. The test set gives one final, honest check. The trouble starts when the validation folds are used to make hundreds of decisions.

Here is an illustrative noisy dataset and a grid of three hundred twelve decision tree settings. The best cross-validated score is point seven five. But the average across all three hundred twelve combinations is only point six seven two. Picking the maximum picked a flattering number.

Why? Each cross-validated score has random error. Try many candidates, choose the highest, and you tend to choose one that got lucky. The winner's score is biased upward, and the more combinations you try, the bigger the effect. The held-out test score here was point seven six seven, but that is one noisy draw from only a hundred twenty rows.

Nested cross-validation fixes the estimate. Put the whole grid search inside an outer cross-validation loop. Each outer fold is scored by a model whose tuning never saw it. Here the five outer scores average point seven oh seven, with a standard deviation of point zero four five. That is the honest number for how this whole tune-and-fit procedure performs.

In each round, hold out one outer fold, run the full search on the rest, score the tuned model on the held-out fold, and finally average. Nested cross-validation estimates performance. Afterward you run a normal search on all the training data to build the final model.

Keep four rules. Tune on training data only, and never let the test set choose anything. Look at the test set once, after every decision is final. Use nested cross-validation when data is scarce. And remember that a smaller search overfits the validation folds less.
